models.name: HRM — Heterogeneous, cementless resurfacing model
models.what_it_computes: Subject-specific proximal femur with density–elasticity mapping from CT, cobalt–chromium cap with porous coating, frictional press-fit contact; computes calcar and greater trochanter load share, femoral neck principal strains, and spatial strain energy density ratios.

models.name: PCR — Parametric, cemented resurfacing model
models.what_it_computes: Cohort-averaged femur geometry with regionally homogeneous cortical/cancellous properties, cobalt–chromium cap with uniform PMMA mantle; computes calcar/neck force fractions, neck bending moment, and zone-wise strain energy density reductions.

mechanisms.name: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Aberrant load paths can elevate femoral neck stress or bypass the calcar, influencing risk of neck fracture and early mechanical failure.

mechanisms.name: Mechanism 2 — Proximal femoral stress shielding
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Chronic reductions in physiologic strain energy density can drive bone resorption, jeopardizing long-term fixation and revision risk.

deviation.detail: All credibility factor attainments are quantified on a 0–100 scale (higher is better), with prespecified acceptance thresholds per mechanism.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
spans: HRM is a subject-specific, cementless press-fit model.

Voxel Hounsfield units (HU) are converted to apparent density ρ via a scanner-specific calibration (ρ = 1.040 + 0.00088 HU g/cm3 for bone-equivalent materials), and mapped to elastic modulus using an established empirical relation E = 10.5 ρ2.29 (GPa) for trabecular bone and E = 17.0 ρ2.0 (GPa) for cortical bone, with a transition across a density threshold of 1.2 g/cm3.

The cementless interface is modeled with finite-sliding surface-to-surface contact between the porous coat and bone, using a penalty contact algorithm with coefficient of friction µ = 0.4 for the initial press-fit.
findings.span: HRM is a subject-specific, cementless press-fit model.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
spans: Convergence criteria combined a residual force norm and energy balance: iterations continued until the residual force fell below 0.3% of the applied force norm and the incremental internal–external energy difference closed within 0.2% of total strain energy.

In HRM, refining the neck and cap rim from 0.8 mm to 0.6 mm reduced peak compressive principal strain at the superior neck by 1.9% for gait and 2.4% for stair ascent, and changed calcar load fraction by 1.3% and 1.5%, respectively.
To probe step-size sensitivity, we reran HRM gait with a fixed increment of 0.05 and of 0.15 at peak load; QOIs differed by less than 0.7% across these schedules.
findings.span: Convergence criteria combined a residual force norm and energy balance: iterations continued until the residual force fell below 0.3% of the applied force norm and the incremental internal–external energy difference closed within 0.2% of total strain energy.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
spans: For stair ascent, HRM MAPE was 11.7% (IQR 9.1–14.4%) with 74% within ±15%.
Under level gait, HRM calcar load fraction was 0.73 versus 0.76 ± 0.06 in tests; under stair ascent, HRM was 0.69 versus 0.71 ± 0.07.
These levels of agreement are consistent with our planned acceptance bands for model–test strain comparisons in mechanism 1.
findings.span: For stair ascent, HRM MAPE was 11.7% (IQR 9.1–14.4%) with 74% within ±15%.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
findings.factor: Relevance of the quantities of interest
spans: The calcar load fraction, neck principal strains, and neck bending moment collectively interrogate whether the resurfaced construct channels force through the head–neck pathway in a manner comparable to intact mechanics and without excess concentration.
Calcar load fraction calibrates the degree of medial buttress engagement—a known determinant of neck safety.

Neck principal strains at rosette-equivalent sites capture the compressive–tensile arcs across the critical cross-section under physiologic loading; these are the local mechanical drivers for initiation of microdamage and crack propagation in the short term.
Neck bending moment quantifies the global lever-arm effect imposed by the cap and any mantle, providing a cross-check that load sharing through the neck remains in family with intact behavior.
findings.span: The calcar load fraction, neck principal strains, and neck bending moment collectively interrogate whether the resurfaced construct channels force through the head–neck pathway in a manner comparable to intact mechanics and without excess concentration.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
findings.factor: Relevance of the validation activities to the COU
spans: Validation activities were structured to mirror the anatomical regions and loading tasks in the COU.
The cadaveric strain gauges were positioned at homologous sites to the model output points in the femoral neck, capturing superior compression and inferior tension during stance tasks.

The load application reproduced both the hip contact vector and abductor line-of-action magnitudes and directions to within planned tolerances, and cap positioning was maintained within a narrow range around the planned values.
findings.span: Validation activities were structured to mirror the anatomical regions and loading tasks in the COU.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
spans: The hip joint contact was applied as a vector of magnitude 2.8 body weight (BW) for level gait and 3.4 BW for stair ascent, acting through the cap’s articular pole.

Loads and positions were mapped to the models using affine transformations constrained by head center, neck axis, and greater trochanter landmarks; resulting positional errors were below 1.5 mm across landmarks.
Mapping of test conditions to models thus preserved the dominant loading directions and magnitudes in the COU while bounding minor discrepancies from fixture compliance and cap positioning variation.
findings.span: The hip joint contact was applied as a vector of magnitude 2.8 body weight (BW) for level gait and 3.4 BW for stair ascent, acting through the cap’s articular pole.

findings.factor: Relevance of the quantities of interest
spans: Region-wise SED ratio and the percentage of bone area below a low-strain threshold function as proxies for Wolffian remodeling drivers.
The threshold of 200 microstrain is consistent with published ranges below which bone resorption is likely in the presence of normal remodeling.
Aggregating SED ratios by zones (calcar, superior and inferior neck, greater trochanter) retains spatial specificity aligned with both clinical intuition and testable regions in the phantom.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
spans: PCR is a cohort-averaged, cemented model created from a statistical shape model of 50 adult femora scaled to match the median neck-shaft angle (128 degrees) and anteversion (12 degrees).
The mantle is perfectly bonded to both the cap and the prepared femoral surface (tie constraints), consistent with a uniform cementing technique.
findings.span: PCR is a cohort-averaged, cemented model created from a statistical shape model of 50 adult femora scaled to match the median neck-shaft angle (128 degrees) and anteversion (12 degrees).

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
spans: Convergence criteria combined a residual force norm and energy balance: iterations continued until the residual force fell below 0.3% of the applied force norm and the incremental internal–external energy difference closed within 0.2% of total strain energy.
Nonlinearities were mild-to-moderate in HRM due to contact and frictional effects; PCR was nominally linear except for minor geometric stiffening.
For PCR, the difference was less than 0.5% across fixed and adaptive schedules.

findings.mechanism: Mechanism 1 — Primary load transfer through the resurfaced femoral head/neck
spans: For PCR, level gait MAPE was 14.2% (IQR 5 plicit FEA credibility 10.4–18.9%) with 68% within ±15%, and stair ascent MAPE was 17.6% (IQR 13.8–21.3%) with 61% within ±15%.
PCR showed 0.67 versus 0.70 ± 0.07 in gait and 0.65 versus 0.68 ± 0.08 in stair ascent, consistent with a stiffer head–mantle composite bypassing a small fraction of calcar load.
These levels of agreement are consistent with our planned acceptance bands for model–test strain comparisons in mechanism 1.

spans: Both models were solved using an implicit quasi-static procedure with full Newton–Raphson iterations and automatic load incrementation.

Convergence criteria combined a residual force norm and energy balance: iterations continued until the residual force fell below 0.3% of the applied force norm and the incremental internal–external energy difference closed within 0.2% of total strain energy.
For both models, we recorded the maximum displacement corrections per iteration; no increment required more than 10 iterations to converge, and the majority converged in 4–6 iterations.
We verified that the artificial work due to stabilization in HRM remained below 0.08% of total work in all increments.
